objects: accuracy of genetic-risk estimates; phenotypic sample size
assumptions: Genome-wide prediction with large numbers of markers
conclusion: Deterministic equations are needed to expose how accuracy determinants interact because simulation-based precision assessment is costly and does not reveal those interactions.
scope: Motivation for analytical accuracy predictions rather than a new effect-estimation procedure.
span: Wray et al. [9] computed the precision of the individual genetic risk estimates by simulation. While simulation studies are useful in getting initial results on the number of phenotypic records needed to achieve a desired level of accuracy, they are computer intensive and time consuming with large numbers of markers. Most importantly, they do not provide a deep insight on how all variables that affect accuracy interact. Therefore, it is desirable to develop deterministic equations that are responsive to all variables that influence accuracy.

objects: continuous phenotype; binary disease status; continuous liability
assumptions: Population study with random sampling, followed by extensions to disease and case-control sampling
conclusion: The derivation starts with a continuous phenotype and extends it to a dichotomous phenotype generated by an underlying continuous liability.
scope: Disease-risk accuracy derived through the liability model.
span: We will first derive equations that are predictive of rgĝ for a genome-wide approach with a continuous phenotype, such as height, assuming a population study where individuals are sampled at random. These will then be adapted to predict disease risk for a dichotomous phenotype (‘affected’ or ‘unaffected’) with an underlying continuous liability. The equations are then further adapted to the situation of case control data.

objects: nG potential loci; additive genetic value
conclusion: Potential trait loci are assumed independent, biallelic and additive, with candidate loci allowed to have zero effects.
scope: Continuous-trait derivation and its disease extensions.
span: We will assume that there are nG potential loci affecting a trait which are independent, biallelic and acting additively, where nG may be large. These loci may be candidate genes or genetic markers of which a significant proportion may have zero effects.

objects: allele frequencies pj; substitution effects beta_j
assumptions: Reference-allele frequencies are symmetric about one half and effects about zero by allele coding
conclusion: The derivation imposes no further distributional assumptions on allele frequencies or effects and allows negligible or zero effects, without imposing covariance restrictions in population samples.
scope: Distributional specification for the population derivation; this is not a fitted Bayesian prior.
span: We shall assume without loss of generality that the distribution of allele frequencies pj is symmetric about p = ½, and likewise that allelic effects βj are symmetric about β = 0. No further distributional assumptions will be made here on pj and βj, so for example, many of the allele segregating may have negligible or zero effect. No assumptions are made concerning the covariance between pj and βj in the populations sampled.

objects: rgĝ; true and predicted genetic values
assumptions: Effects estimated in one population sample and applied to another sample from the same population
conclusion: Accuracy is the correlation between true and predicted genetic values, and the derived prediction represents an attainable upper bound under the stated estimation and population setting.

span: The predicted accuracy that is derived below represents the upper bound that can be achieved when estimating effects in one population sample and then predicting individual genetic risk in another sample from the same population. Throughout this article the accuracy of predicted genetic risk (rgĝ) is defined as the correlation between true and predicted genetic values.

objects: cross-population prediction; var(xij); allele frequency; admixture; epistasis
assumptions: Effects estimated in one population and predictions transferred to another
conclusion: Transfer accuracy depends on genotype variation in both populations and may be impaired by changed allele frequencies, admixture or epistatic effects.
scope: The same-population calculation does not settle cross-population accuracy.
span: Specifically, the ability to transfer predictions will depend on var(xij) in each of the two populations used for estimation and application, and this in turn depends on both the allele frequency (pj) and the degree of admixture present in the population. Furthermore, an additional risk of transferability across populations is the presence of epistasis which may differentially influence βj.

objects: genome-wide risk prediction; marker inclusion; significance threshold
assumptions: Comparison of the earlier genome-wide approaches discussed in the introduction
conclusion: Wray et al. select disease-prediction loci by a significance threshold, whereas Meuwissen et al. use all loci regardless of their trait effects.
scope: Author-stated comparison of earlier methods motivating genome-wide prediction.
span: One critical difference between the two genome-wide approaches is that Wray et al. [9] set a significance threshold for the loci selected for disease prediction, whereas Meuwissen et al. [10] use all loci regardless of whether they affect or not the trait considered. The approach of Meuwissen et al. [10] therefore attempts to achieve the maximum estimate precision of the complete genetic value for a given dataset by including loci that may have too small of an effect to achieve statistical significance, and, thus, reduces the overestimation of allele effects [12].
